policy: Runaway and hypervelocity stars fast enough to leave the Milky Way. Gaia DR3 parallaxes cannot place them, so each is placed at its spectroscopic distance; that distance stands in for the parallax, so that its Gaia DR3 proper motion and measured radial velocity give its motion through space.

stars.name: S5-HVS1
stars.distance_note: 8630 ± 300 pc, the spectro-photometric distance (log D/kpc = 0.936 ± 0.015) of Koposov et al. 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.11725; if the star started at Sagittarius A*, its orbit requires 8884 ± 11 pc. The Gaia DR3 parallax, 0.035 ± 0.040 mas, does not constrain it

astrometry.astrometry_ref: Position and proper motion Gaia DR3, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.00211; the parallax is the inverse of the spectro-photometric distance of Koposov et al. 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.11725
astrometry.radial_velocity_ref: Heliocentric radial velocity from AAT/2dF and follow-up spectra, Koposov et al. 2020

stars.note: The fastest main-sequence hypervelocity star found by 2019, an A-type star leaving the Milky Way at 1755 +55/−45 km/s in the Galactic rest frame. Traced back, its orbit leads unambiguously to the Galactic Center: Sagittarius A* flung it out about 4.8 million years ago at about 1800 km/s (Koposov et al. 2020). Its path and travel time match the disk of young stars around Sagittarius A*. A mass of 2.35 ± 0.06 M_sun and an age of about 50 million years (log age 7.72 +0.25/−0.33) come from isochrones fitted to its spectrum and photometry; they are model values and not adopted.

stars.name: US 708
stars.distance_note: 8500 ± 1000 pc, the spectroscopic distance for the canonical 0.3 M_sun of a helium star, Geier et al. 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.01650. The Gaia DR3 parallax, 0.067 ± 0.204 mas, does not constrain it

astrometry.astrometry_ref: Position and proper motion Gaia DR3, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.00211; the parallax is the inverse of the spectroscopic distance of Geier et al. 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.01650
astrometry.radial_velocity_ref: Coadded Keck/ESI spectrum, Geier et al. 2015

stars.note: A helium-rich hot subdwarf (spectral class He-sdO) and one of the fastest stars known to be leaving the Milky Way. It is probably the surviving companion of a thermonuclear supernova: it fed a white dwarf in an orbit of about 10 minutes until the white dwarf exploded and released it at its orbital speed. Tides in that tight orbit spun it up; it still rotates at 115 ± 8 km/s (projected). Its surface gravity is log g = 5.69 ± 0.09. Geier et al. 2015 derived 1157 ± 53 km/s in the Galactic rest frame from ground-based proper motions (−8.0 ± 1.8, +9.1 ± 1.6 mas/yr). Gaia DR3 measures a smaller, far more precise proper motion, which lowers its speed across the sky; a 2023 reanalysis with Gaia still finds it unbound (Heber et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.02969). The mass of 0.3 M_sun is assumed for a helium star, not measured, and is not adopted.
